open_obligations: Check the share of confidently wrong answers under debate, not only the Brier score.
Note the domain differs (contested health claims vs MMLU and QuALITY).
Check whether overconfidence differs by prior-belief group.

Note the protocol and evidence differ: Bowman et al.'s observation comes from a simple human-model interaction protocol with a single model and is qualitative ('sometimes'), while Rahman et al. measure calibration under debate and consultancy.
out.other_title: Participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgments and sometimes accept confident-sounding false model claims
out.rationale: Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give highly confident wrong judgements. Rahman et al. report judges are overconfident under both debate and consultancy, with overconfidence most pronounced at confidence levels above 80%, but debate gives better calibration (Brier 0.231 vs 0.335); the setting is AI debate and consultancy on controversial claims.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether human judges assisted by AI are overconfident, for debate versus consultancy on COVID-19 claims

open_obligations: Check the calibration curve above 80% confidence under debate alone.
Note judges hold strong priors, unlike Michael et al.'s near-50/50 judges.
Check that Brier differences are not driven by accuracy differences alone.
out.other_title: Debate may not extract all knowledge; too-complex arguments could stalemate the judge
out.rationale: Michael et al. find calibration difficult in the high-confidence regime. Rahman et al. report judges are overconfident under both debate and consultancy, most above 80% confidence, while debate improves Brier score (0.231 vs 0.335); this supports the difficulty and shows debate only partly helps.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether human judges of AI debate are well calibrated at high confidence, on COVID-19 claims
